Reviews.136567:
What the people that say "you've played x number of hours why give it a negative?" don't understand is that when you're putting in the hours, it feels like there is a point.  All the grinding, exploring, trading, etc. make you feel like there is a huge universe to explore and you can do anything.  And it's sort of true.  Galaxies and systems are fun to explore and it's amazing to fly from space into atmosphere and land on a planet without load screens. You can upgrade your ship, base, weapon, vehicles, suit and you can even on and manage a fleet.

You spend all that time thinking if I had a bigger ship, I could store more inventory and then really get going, or if my base was a bit bigger, I could do xyz and then I'll finally be where I want to be, etc. But then you eventually realize that that's all there is.  

The universe only feels big but everything is generally the same.  The planets look different and that feels good, but you eventually notice it's just resources, ruins, plants and animals to scan on every one--Nothing interesting to do, no cool people to meet and adventure with. Most of the missions are basically scan this or kill that and it doesn't even matter what planet you do it on.  Every space station is basically the same and the NPCs are nearly pointless copies of each other and not capable of any meaningful interaction.

The feeling that you can do anything eventually fades as you see through the facade and notice that there's nothing behind it.  The hours you put into this game are enjoyable only because you are tricked into feeling like there is more to it than there is.  While you are in that zone, it really is enjoyable and even after that you can have fun with what you've built.  But it's hard to give this game a positive review because of the inevitable disappointment that comes when you pull back the curtain and see that the Great and Powerful Oz is just some con man.

I was one of the rare few people who really dove into and enjoyed the day one release version of this game and accumulated a good 200-300 hours. The game could get boring and grindy pretty fast back then, but my days of playing MMORPGs had gotten me accustomed to boring grinds. 
What I really enjoyed about No Man's Sky was the space travel, the space combat(again, many would probably disagree with me there, but I liked it), the exploration, the MASSIVE planets, the amazing art style and visuals, and just the mysterious overtone in which it felt like you were gathering bits and pieces of the story of different races and learning that many of them were connected in various ways, and then suddenly you get into these anomalies just randomly floating about in space that seem to herald some type of space geezus mystery......... it was just a really unique experience overall. 
With every positive though comes some negatives, yes the game was grindy as hell, and yes the inventory space thing was a real annoyance, combined with the fact that there didn't seem to be any clearly defined goals and that the grind didn't seem to have much of a purpose, the assets were apparently in short supply and after a while started looking way too similar and it seemed like there was way too much copy/pasting going on between all of the procedeurally(yes I'm too lazy to spell check) generated worlds, and there wasn't alot to do outside of the grind, and then there's that $60 price tag.... there was enough content to maybe justify half of that, but in no way was the game worth the price of a full featured AAA game.
Eventually after several hundred hours in the release version I burned out and had to step back for a while, the whole time though watching the progress of the game and seeing how dedicated the developers were to trying to make sure people got what they paid for, turning this into a game worthy of sinking several hundred hours into....... fast forward to today, a pandemic outbreak, most of us stuck at home with not alot to do, the game was on sale, and I thought why not give it another go? Definitely not regretting that so far.

I have only played for 20 hours and I feel like I haven't even scratched the surface. I love the exploration part of this game as well as the real feeling of having to watch my resources to be sure I can actually get back to my base (or a space station). 
However, I do feel like the flora and fauna are very similar on every planet I visit. For example, the animals all seem to be some iteration of 'slug thing': same rubbery texture, color scheme and basic formula of familiar yet alien. Mind you, I haven't explored too much yet but so far that seems to be it. No furry things, no scaled things, nothing super mind blowing or unique. (Cute, for sure. The slug rhino-pigs are my faves so far.)
The main quest has been a definite help on my first playthrough and I'm getting more comfortable with the controls, which can be a little all over the place. Once you get the hang of it the controls do become second nature and there's a certain flow to flying and landing as well as recharging your tech, switching multitool functions, and so on. There have been a couple of moments where I was lost on exactly what to do but having a look in my inventory usually solved it since things tend to blink and glow if they're important at that moment.
Overall No Man's Sky has been fun and I would recommend it to anyone looking for an exploration/survival game that doesn't totally hold your hand.

I love this game. That doesn't mean you will.
If you're looking for an incredible, quest-filled, action-packed space explorer...this isn't the game for you. It still feels like there's a lot missing from this game, although the devs do a great job of adding new things all the time. However, there are still LOADS of unresolved issues. Combat gets stale, you eventually start seeing the same planets over and over again, exploration gets boring, ship upgrading gets annoying, the quests are bland from the start.

However, if you're like me, none of that matters. I've always wanted to be able to explore the stars. To hop in a ship and go anywhere I wanted, whenever I wanted. I loved watching Star Wars, and seeing our heroes travel around the galaxy. I wanted to do that! I wanted my own ship, and the freedom to go anywhere. No restrictions, no responsiblities, just freedom and endless possibilities. For me, it's not just about the gameplay, it's about the experience. It's filled a niche that no other game could. Starbound was a lot of fun, but it wasn't quite fulfilling my dreams. No Man's Sky was exactly what I wanted.

Would I tell my friends to buy No Man's Sky? No. I wouldn't. I won't deny that it is VERY far from perfect.
But that doesn't mean I think it's a bad game.

Reviews.136677:
I LOVE THIS GAME


I seriously do. this game has everything you would want in a perfect game. Except it's not perfect. For the first few dozen hours I was just astonished by the stunning visuals of space, a disbelief on how the 'procedural generation' thing actually worked so fine, and just the feeling that I'm able to do anything in this infinite unexplored universe.


But as you progress through the game, you come to this dead end, where you realize that this infinite universe you were promised with, is actually a vast emptiness with little things to do actually do game-wise.


First things first, the bugs. There are A LOT of bugs, or some discomfort due to pour development. There aren't any game-breakingly horrible ones but the bugs feel like mosquitoes, where they'll make you itch and will make disturbing and annoying noises around your ears whilst your sweet bedtime. It will cut the dramatic emotions during this unbelievably gorgeous scenery and will bring considerable disruption and frustration to your gameplay. And for me, I got used to it somehow, but for some this surely will be quite an obstacle.


And for the game itself, it's actually really good early on. But they will fall in interest soon after. There are a whole lot of variety in the elements and material that you collect and all have pretty unique sprite and cool names which i really liked, but they lack versatility in their uses. This will directly lead to the gameplay, which in the late game, there is no actual need to use the multitools for mining uses, which removes one of the core mechanics of the game itself.


The crafting mechanics are also a huge disappointment. With so many elements and crafting materials in hand, you can't help but wonder 'What sorts of cool sh!t will I be able to make with these sick stuff that I collected'. But the heartbreak truth is that other than some techs that you can attach on your exosuit, spaceships, multitool and freighter, there aren't much of a use for crafting and refining.


This ties in with the ultimate problem, lack of 'ACTUAL' content. I haven't played this game a lot yet, and surely haven't exhaust all the things I can do in this game. But as I said, the crafting mechanic doesn't have much use other than upgrading techs and... money. Most of the high technology available in the end game is all, ALL for trading purposes, which means their only use is to sell on the market for money, but I don't mean that money ain't important in this game. Money is of course very important in No Man's Sky. They're used all the time, as for example buying a ship, buying the upgrade parts, expanding your inventory size, and... and... and that's the problem. There are so little to do with the game and yet it's scarce content forces you to earn money, even though there are such less use for it.


Lastly, I want to discuss about lack of reward for exploration, and lack of things to explore as well. Exploration is the key part in this game, as it half-forces you on your exploration as early on as the beginning of the game. You'll explore your first planet and will find this fascinating procedurally generated planet with plants and animals, which looks so magical and alien. You'll explore, find ruined buildings, find recipes, and the game so far is fantastic. The elements you get while you explore will make one curious as the alien NPCs will make you even more curious. The game will give you so many questions to be answered, but you are no more than an inch away from finding out that the answer is nowhere to be found. The procedurally generated biomes have too little variety for a game of such scale. Animals and plants will look fabulous until you realize their only use is to be harvested or fed for materials. And the NPCs are no more than either a merchant or a walking disposable dictionaries. Of course I want to mention the NPCs found in the small bases on the surface which has astonishingly well written dialogue, with extra detail to answer to pick depending on the alien's race. The depots and facilities which sentinels guard and the 'biological horrors' are a amazing addition to the things-to-explore-list but they all end up with the same problem, which is the rewards being insufficient in where to use. That is the core problem. You have quite a lot of things to do(I still think there should be much, MUCH more added), but their rewards will be disappointing for the most of the time. Your progress and effort won't really show up on your gameplay. And as you proceed through the game you'll feel there are no reason to explore anymore. A depressing halt will come to you as you realize, that this endless sky is for no man. 


The game after a few 70 or more hours feel so shallow than what you would expect. It was supposed to be a game would and could fulfill everything all gaming scene have wanted. But it barely couldn't reach that height.... just yet.


I'm aware that this state of the game I'm able to play is an immense improvement from what it has been on it's first release. I would fall short of words praising Shawn and Hello Games for their fascinating job and the neverending effort to make the game better. I'm still looking forward to updates and bug-fixes I really enjoy this game and recently started a new game on creative. I could not find another game that excited me in the ways that No Man's Sky did. I truly fell in love with this game, but I think it could be something that no man has ever made. 


I'm looking forward to more updates, and my simple thoughts are;
-Fix the minor, the smallest of bugs and inconvenience factors first. Such as being unable to know which frigate is damaged and needs to be repaired.
-Add new mechanics to reward players for crafting high level items. An improvement to the crafting system is needed as well(it is so hard to remember and discriminate each ingredient, and especially Magno-gold and Carbon Crystal)
-Add variety to things to explore and the rewards they give. Also make more usage for the money so many people are making from their 'activated indium farm'.

[h1] tl;dr: I will continue playing the game, because I have fun playing the game. But you need a lot of frustration tolerance to enjoy it. [/h1]

First of all: [/b] I really like this game. [/b]

It is mostly great fun, you can explore a lot, it has this certain feeling of not being able to stop because there is so much more to do.

BUT! There are [b] a lot [/b] of bugs and really anoying mechanics, that makes playing this game actually a painful experience every once in a while.
EG 1: I played a mission with 2 friends, died and respawned somewhere in a random sector. To this point, no problem. But then I tried to enter the anomaly (some kind of multiplayer hive thingy) and the game crushed at the exact moment I tried to leave my spaceship. Again and again.

EG 2: I tried to build my base out of different sets of components, only to recognise that the sets of components do not match to each other, so you can not attach them. That leads to painfully imprecise manually attaching, or, even worse, random notifications of [i] "you can not place this here" [/i]

EG 3: Random soundbugs in multiplayer (nearby spaceships of group members continue to make unbearable noices)

EG 4: The HUD just doesn't show the correct quest locations, or, even better, shows quest locations for quests that are not active.

EG 5: Overall just not comprehensible multiplayer mechanics. This, I admit, is slightly subjective, and maybe I am just not a very smart guy. But time after time I found myself wondering, why the game acted in a certain way, or, worse, won't act the way I expected it to do. (questing together, using bases, joining sessions, etc etc)

In addition, there were plenty of minor bugs and problems I can not and will not list here, but i think, you got the point.

Purchased this for VR. It actually looks like a good port, apart from two major problems.


The game does not support room-scale VR (360° turning). What this means is the HUD is always locked in one direction. If you turn in real life, it will be behind you. You must use snap turning or smooth turning to play this.

Secondly, there is no option for head-based movement. You can choose between teleportation or hand movement, which requires you to point where you want to walk. That is the deal breaker for me, it's infuriating.


Otherwise, from the 15 minutes I played, I was impressed. This isn't a half arsed Bethesda port, you have some real interaction. You equip the mining tool off your back, there are wrist menu's, actual cockpit controls, etc.

It is one small patch away from being a game I can see myself playing a lot of, but not gonna hold my breath, they've had a long time already.

This is not a bad game. You can spend countless hours playing it.  You won't be doing much though.

   No Man's Sky has definitely improved since it's launch. Lot's of features have been added or revamped. The issue is that there is very little depth in most of the features. Land and Sea vehicles were added, and aside from races are not able to do anything that your ship could do from the start of the game. Once all of the main quests are complete all that is left to do is wandering around on increasingly similar planets, doing the same missions from space stations over and over again, and base building. Of that, only 1 is rewarding enough to carry the game.

    Base Building is really where this game shines. There is almost no limit to what you can do if you have the time and creativity. Near the end-game you will spend all of your time either maintaining your base or gathering materials to expand it. If that is what you are into, this game has you covered. If not, you still have to participate as the farms you can create are able to create more money than you will know what to do with.

   The additions the developers have added are great, yet aspects of the game which were promised before the launch still go uncovered. Living ships are cool, but a more robust faction system would be cooler.

The game is enjoyable on many fronts. It's all great until you decide you want it all and realize you can't have it. Not unless you want to blow your brains out half way through.  Kudos to the devs that keep coming up  with new and interesting content to keep what is essentially an exploration game fresh. 
BUT the amount of glitches and bugs, broken main quest lines and mini quests, and base building/farming objects that just don't work correctly is embarrassingly large. Normally I would have given a positive review but after 200+ hours of game play, waiting for glitches to be fixed and game objects to function correctly, it seems that they most likely never will. 
It's an impressive game really but it still feels like it should still be in Beta because  they keep releasing small and large content updates without fixing day one bugs.

TLDR: 
 Subnautica meets Minecraft.

Excellent single player for about 50 hours. 
Multiplayer is very buggy and crashes a lot. Expensive items are randomly lost in machines. Worth the 60 USD to go through it. One shouldn't expect it to be fun for more than that.
........................................

  Breath of fresh air for someone sitting at home looking for something to do on downtime.  The concept is some new age some old school put together to form a chill kind of game.  
  The game should be played in a way that fits the player.  If you want to build a huge base on a planet that you love, amass a HUGE storage of resources, kill pirates  with a customized super badass ship or just run about with friends and enjoy each others company, it's all there for you.  
  If you're a min maxer and focus on end, this game will be very grindy and is not for you as the rewards are very lackluster.
With nms it's all about the climb. If you find yourself sitting at the computer looking over your list of games and say 'yeah, i dont wanna do that. I don't wanna do that either...' to every game in your library- as i so often do-  then its worth the play through till you find another game to play when you get to that point again.

Overall .. Good game with low replay value because of the bugs and crashes.

Reviews.137088:
No Man's Sky has changed dramatically over the years.
It first started out as a big empty promise, which I'm sure no one will forget. It later slowly turned into much more than what they originally claimed.
The potential of this game is astounding, having many kinds of missions for you to complete, including weekend challenges you can complete with strangers from around the world. There is just so much to do and it provides for a never-ending experience that you just have to see for yourself.
The scale of this game is really eye-opening, making you feel so insignificant as just being a Traveller. There are countless amounts of galaxies, planets, stars, space stations, etc. that really makes you feel as if you have the entire universe at the click of a button, but also there's just so much to explore and uncover throughout your gameplay. Just looking through the galaxy map alone had me left with a feeling no other game could have accomplished. It's almost like a representation of our own universe, just on a smaller-seeming scale.

Origionally purchased on the PS4 at launch, repurchased on PC for next and have been trying to play with every major update since. No Man's Sky is better in many ways from when it first released, but still not very fleshed. VR is a great addition, much better than similar attempts like Skyrim or Fallout. The game looks and runs great on my PC, smooth 60+ fps, and the planets are incredibly vibrant. That said, gameplay annoyingly varies between very chill and intensely aggravating and I still feel like I'm lacking any kind of real end game motivation on my casual profile. Exploration and crafting are very well executed, but combat and survival elements fall flat. I'd wait for a sale. 

On a side note they really need to work on how trash starting planets are, especially on permadeath. Spending over an hour resetting the game trying to find a planet with at least a CAVE I could hide in to catch my breath isn't fun. Creative isn't engaging. I understand the point of the game is to fix your ship and get off of that planet ASAP, but making it completely uninhabitable 100% of the time seems like a poor excuse at providing the player with some sort of sense of urgency, if only for that one planet. In my experience, games usually provide little to no real threats in the first level or so. Being bombarded with resource management and hazards from the second you gain control just seems ass backwards, even for a "survival" game, which is a term i use loosely here.

 Inventory seems like its been sorely neglected despite updates. Why do exosuit and ship mods still take up space? Like isn't your jetpack ALSO your backpack? Why would it take up space? As far as I know it doesn't ever even need to be charged or repaired like other items. To me it would make a hell of a lot more sense to have dedicated inventory space and mod slots, because right now it just makes menu navigation feel sloppy.

Fix the pacing of the early game, make the stats on ships and multitools matter more, fix the inventory system, and you've got a really decent space survival exploration sim. Really happy to see how far NMS has come, it so clearly launched way before it had any right to be a full priced game on store shelves. Unfortunately though, it still feels much like an early access experience at the moment, years after it's official launch.

I dont just thumbs up lightly. Its a cool game, good graphics, VR support. Love the vehicles.

But once you been to the 5 or 7 types of planets, you pretty much been to all of them.  

Personally I dont like all the number of quests, I dont like the story, I dont like the lore.

But the base building is legit, the visuals are tight... but once you leave the planet, it really spits on science, I dont even know where to begin... the distance from planets, the asteroid fields being retardedly and unrealisicly dense and everywhere.  Attacks from pirates every 5 seconds, basically dont goto space, but to get somewhere.

Once in a planet atmo, its pretty imersive, and well done, and those views can be amazing... even a few choice moments in space can happen, like when you warp in your capital ship. or look at a window at your fleet in orbit of the planet.

The galaxy is teaming with life, so how are you the first to discover anything?  Every place you go, there is NPCs flying by every 5min.   My first moment in the game, I was a crashed ship dude on a unknown planet, and I kept seeing people fly over me.... pretty silly.

The universe just doesn't feel unique, or special anywhere you go, its the same, for the most part.  Some planets have a few neat things, but its all cosmetic.  

Its grind.. but its not hard.. there isn't any here tech tree to work for.. The only real unlock is done buy going to 4 types of stars for their unique metals.

One thing I didn't like, you spend a good portion of your time playing, deciding what to keep and what to sell because the inventory system is very restrictive and limited, so there is going to be a lot of sorting, and you can't just build more storage like in minecraft.  

I eventally got bored with the story line, and the endless quests.... got the game on sale for 25 bucks... and for that its worth it i'd say though.

PC 2D: 7/10 ---PC VR: 11/10

I was born in 1980; there, I am a "boomer." That said, I AM the one who waits, doesn't pre-order, hates EA, and all the things that you newbie runts take for granted. Now to the review...

When this game was initially announced, my brother and I said if they could deliver just half of what was promised; it would be an epic game. That didn't happen; BUT, that wasn't the end. I have put 1000+ hrs into Elite: Dangerous, XBox, PC, and PCVR (Oculus). I love Elite; however, it did begin to feel like a chore/job, to just have enough money to replace what I would burn up on fun raids/missions. I felt like I had to toil a bit too much for the fun part of the game; the loop was/is busted a bit. Still love that game though! I wanted an Elite: Dangerous "Lite" and that is what NMS delivers.

This could almost be a review split into two, though. As a base, PC game; I find it a bit above average. As a VR game though; it is an out of the park, walk-off, grand slam. Seriously, if you want space legs in ED and are tired of waiting, NMS is your answer! I too, was finally persuaded to get this game when I saw how much had gone into it since I had blocked this utter disappointment from my brain. Roll forward to the Internet Historian, a few other videos (KrazeGamer, etc) I decided to finally get it on sale. I have 400+ hours into it, and will easily surpass my ED time. IF, they ever get space legs I will consider going back. For now, my go to game in VR is NMS; easily the best VR experiences that exist.

On a side note: Why isn't every XBox 360/PS3 era game made into a VR experience?!? The port would be worth the time and effort; AAA games would be made VR, and everyone would win. 

PC/Desktop: Recommend, if you like Minecraft in Space. 
VR: Get it already. This game SHOULD be the flagship game right now. It is nice to see HL:Alyx bringing some much needed attention back to VR.

Great game! Never played it at release because I saw so many negative reviews, saw Internet Historians video and decided to give it a go.

Graphics:
 Graphics are great (mostly), except for VR (which still isn't half bad), and when terrain occasionally doesn't fully load (it won't mess up the game really, just kinda look odd). Mostly though, planets will just look plain epic.

Multiplayer:
 Multiplayer is ehh... Ok. It tends to be very laggy and you'll have items disappearing from refiners every once in a while, when you build stuff, it tends to disappear then reappear like 10 seconds later. Although, multiplayer does add alot to the experience, the nexus is awesome too, doing missions with other people is really nice.

Gameplay:
 Oh boi, I love the gameplay, it may feel grindy to some people, which, at times is is kinda grindy not gonna lie. I just built farms for almost every resource and starting buying everything else, making myself able to build giant bases with no problem. I didn't feel any boredom at all till at least 100 hours in. I can still get on and play though because they keep adding constant updates and such.

VR:
 VR is awesome in this game, graphics are still not bad and you still get the whole experience. You can still fly spacecrafts and drive exocrafts (though it is hard to get used too). Building is also fine in VR too, but to my knowledge you cant go into build cam.

Final thots:
 I think more updates would be sick, so thank goodness they're still active on developing the game. I think it's worth the money, but it's mostly down to personal preference. You want a semi-grindy game with space ships , building, big cars with laser, and giant evil walking robots? Then it's perfect for you.

When I first bought this game I was looking forward to exploring other planets the most, so needless to say I was taken aback when I logged in and realized that I had to do some tutorial on ground and find and fix my gear and ship before I could start exploring. Thankfully that part of the tutorial wasn't too brutal and I was up and flying in no time. 
 The graphics and content are both awesome, with a lot of side missions you can opt to do as well. 
  My 2 biggest pet peeves with this game continue to be the (unreasonably long) length of time to load the game, and the amount of time it takes to Warp/Teleport anywhere, in my opinion those activities should never take more than 1 minute to complete, however I find that the average time it takes is about 2.5 minutes, and occasionally up to 5 minutes. Hopefully the developers will be able to fix this soon. 
  Loving the new living ship update with new Living Tech that you can install, however I wish there was a way to install scanners in them for Conflict and Economy detecting, as it stands right now there is no way to do this with the Living Ships.
  Speaking of ships I love the variety of classes and styles there are and the upgrade ability is great as well.
  Overall I would have to say this game gets 8 out of 10 Stars from me because of the sheer variety of options you have, and the endless amount of systems you can explore. As well as the ability to play with your friends. If the developers could fix the length of time it takes the game to load, as well as the length of time it takes to Teleport and Warp places I would give this game 10 out of 10 stars. I have put so many hours into this game it is totally addicting.

Sincerely,
Bodi420

Reviews.137571:
Perhaps the best gaming comeback story of all time. When I first downloaded NMS I got the same bad taste in my mouth that 90% of community got and an overwhelming sense of a missed opportunity. Here was a game that definitely suffered from over hype and had me really excited to explore this world. The structure, aesthetic, and basic gameplay were all as advertised; eye catching, exotic, and rife with the infinite options of a procedurally generated galaxy. But after that; a profoundly shallow experience that was not at all what we were led to expect from the developer. I promptly refunded. 

Fast forward two years and to my utter disbelief I see NMS trending again with very good recent reviews and as soon as I took a look at what Hello Games had managed to achieve with the “NEXT” and other updates, I eagerly jumped back in feet first. What was once a hollow grindy experience had been fully fleshed out in to an incredible living breathing world with a host of fun and engaging opportunities to explore (base building, farming, trading, fleet management, etc etc) and a much more developed central plot. As they stated themselves; this was what the game was meant to be and I am incredibly impressed in the Hello team that they stuck to their guns and made it happen. What was once a gimmicky flashy title without much substance was now a galactic epic, sure to hook players for years to come. 

If you’ve ever looked up at night and thought what wonders all those stars must hold, this is definitely a game you’ll want to check out.

It is well established that this game had a rough launch. I don't think anyone would defend it, but Hello Games didn't abandon this title or their vision. 

The game in its current state (writing this as of Living Ship update) is unrecognizable from what it was at launch. It took a few years, but Hello Games have actually delivered on their original promises, and even added new features which weren't even on the roadmap during the hype-train on its release. 

I am a big fan of space games/exploration, and have played pretty much every title out there relating to these categories. There is, frankly, nothing else out there like it. It may not be for you, but if it clicks, it will be a unique and incredible gaming experience that you cannot get anywhere else. This is especially apparent in its VR implementation: this is one of the best VR titles out there. The interface was completely overhauled to support it from the ground up, and after the major bugs were worked out after its initial introduction (mostly relating to performance optimization issues) the game could be regarded as the standard for post-launch VR introduction. 

Make no mistake, this game isn't perfect. There are still bugs. There are still some baffling design decisions. The biggest strength, then, is Hello Games continued dedication and development towards their product. They clearly believe in this thing, and it shows.

This game has come a long way since it first released. I preordered it and quit playing a few days after launch. The controls were awkward while the gamplay was shallow and failed to deliver on so many levels. However since then the devs have worked hard to improve nearly every aspect of the game. It still has some work to do, but I am glad I gave it another chance. 
Some of my complaints are as follows: Despite the near limitless number of systems and planets, it doesnt take long for much of the game to look very familiar. The flora, fauna, starships and buildings seem to be generated from a limited pool of pieces randomly stitched together, and the terrain could use a lot of love. Each planet type has its own visual theme but once you have seen one, the rest look very similar despite being procedurally generated. The jetpack can be awkward and trying to control your ship in space is a near soul destroying experience.
That being said the game really does look beautiful, and it is still a lot of fun finding your feet in a huge universe full of systems and planets to visit and soo many things to scan. It can be a lot of fun exploring new planets, upgrading your suit, weapon and starship and even building a base if you are into that. The Nexus has added limited multiplayer and the game is adding new features for free as they create them.
I have happily spent hours exploring the universe and can finally say I have gotten my moneys worth out of this game after all this time. The game is far from perfect, but it WILL entertain you if you give it the chance. I'm excited to see what the future will bring for this game.

TLDR; End game is still a little weak, but a LOT of fun getting there. Give it a try. 8.5/10

I thought the first few hours of this game were quite fun, but little did I know how much of the actual game formula would be repeated ad nauseam from that point forward. This entire game, from collecting materials to the quests themselves, is just one big game of fetch in the most repetitive and uninspired way possible.

Some of the point-to-point travel is so mind-numbingly boring that it takes anywhere from 30-40 seconds of autopilot warp speed travel to reach your destination, followed by 20 seconds of manually flying your ship down to the planet itself. What is the point of this? If this was a loading screen it wouldn't be tolerable, so why is this okay? Flying and landing your ship has to be a grandiose, delayed animated spectacle every single time.

Dialogue and notifications are very slow and there's no real "fast-forward" button; you're along for the ride of listening to the same three alien grunting noises over and over whether you like it or not. Ending one dialogue option generally closes the entire dialogue menu, rather than bringing you back to the menu. Space stations are unnecessarily large and divided into two sections, and no running is allowed because that would just be rude.

Certain side quests have actual 2-5hr timers placed on them before you can progress. Why? Because this game clearly tries its hardest to test your patience for no real reason.

The primary "threat" of the game is a force of Sentinels whose scripting completely breaks when (not if) they decide to fly inside the doors of your base. They will just float around confused and lost and pretend you don't exist. Meanwhile, Sentinel Quads disregard all physics and terrain and will leap through literally everything to headbutt and blast you with laser beams. Walkers will, well, walk right through your base and often push you away from whatever you're trying to do inside your base.

The quest menu and tracker is horrible. Certain quests aggressively take precedence over anything else you're doing even if they have no real urgency (looking at you, pirate bounty quests). You cannot track any other quest until you've arbitrarily flown off-planet and killed the pirate (which is probably bugged itself and just idling indefinitely) to complete the quest. Sorting through quests is both tedious and confusing with the terrible and limited quest menu.

Stay away from this game. They had three years since release and it's still a mess.

This game is so. Expansive.

Okay, let's start from the beginning. [SPOILERS ALERT]

You start with your memories forgotten and a starship that has crashed into the planet you currently inhabit. After following through some tutorial bits that teach yu base mechanics such as mining, terraforming, and using materials to craft and repair things, you eventually gain the ability to travel to other planets. Reviews.137737: First everyone was hyped for this game and could't wait to play it, then when it came out everyone hated it. Now that Hello Games has released a whole bunch of free patches and expansions for it, everybody likes it again. But there's more necessary for me to like a game then just getting free expansions, the game must also be fun to play! I can't even say that No Man's Sky is really fun in the first couple of hours. Sure everything is still new and there's lots of stuff to explore but it's just so boring, there's nothing to do. You start the game and first have to get through some poorly designed tutorial, where you keep dying over and over because you keep running out of O2 but can't collect any O2 because you also keep getting poisoned even though you're wearing a space suit. And you can't collect any sodium to recharge you hazmat protection because you keep dying of oxygen deprivation and poison in your face. Anyway, once you get the scanner after your 67th funeral and you can get O2 and sodium out of plants and stuff,  you can leave this poisonous hellhole and never come back. However there are a few problems that lay ahead. The handling of the spaceship is f*cking atrocious and you can't land or take off manually. A game where you're flying a spaceship about 50% of the time really should't make those mistakes. It's the kiss of death for your game. The second major problem is that every time you take off in your spaceship you use the same amount of fuel (about 50% of total capacity), regardless of whether you fly to another planet or your house at the other side of the lake. This forces you to not use your spaceship and go on foot when you have to travel distances of a few kilometers. Which not only takes really long and is boring but pretty much every planet is poisonous you constantly have to recharge your hazmat protection. However, there is a way to avoid having to walk around these poisonous nightmare worlds and that is going through tunnels. Yes you have a tool to dig tunnels and you don't get poisoned while walking through them. The only downside to this is that there is absolutely nothing to find underground and it's more boring walking through the tunnels than on the surface. And even if you can live with all that boredom and terrible game design there is absolutely nothing to do or see once you leave your starting star system. Every planet looks the same and has the same features. There are no rivers, interesting land formations, mountains or forests. I recommend this game to no one. If I had to choose between playing this game or getting fired out of a cannon into the sun, I would choose the cannon. The flying mechanics would be better and I would witness the planets actually orbiting a star, which doesn't happen in No Man's Sky.

Reviews.137884:
It's worth playing, but it still feels like a game that is in beta. There are so many small annoyances, glitches and quality of life improvements needed that it doesn't feel like a complete, well thought out and polished game yet. The economy is easily exploitable so you can reach end game wealth in your first few days of playing. The grindiest part of the game for some reason is unlocking your inventory slots. Ship to ship combat is terrible with the biggest challenge simply being getting your aim sights on the enemy. I found the story somewhat boring and convoluted, but I find most game plots to be badly written...

Positives:
1. It looks nice.
2. Inter-planetary / solar system travel is fast, easy and smooth.
3. Some of the planets / creatures / plants / anomolies are pretty cool the first time you see them.
4. Despite all it's flaws (and there are many!) it's still addictive game play the first time through. This is mainly because you want to unlock things, get a bad-ass ship, get rich, get a capital ship, etc...Not necessarily because there is much fun or challenge in the game play itself.

Negatives:
1. Interplanetary / solar system / galaxy travel is almost too easy to the point it feels like an exploit, due to instant travel anywhere with teleporters. On one hand it's nice that it doesn't take you hours and hours to travel around like for example Elite Dangerous, but on the other hand there is no feeling of distance and immersion and space due to the instant teleporter travel and mere seconds to get to another solar system in your ship.

2. Many planets are just carbon copies of others so after you have seen about a dozen or so different planets, there is no more real reason to explore, which makes the nearly infinite number of planets pointless. More diversity being added in to the planet generation would do wonders for this game by increasing the immersion factor and making exploration worth the time and effort. Of course this is a problem for all games that use procedural map generation...

3. Grinding your inventory slots is a pain. After being 90+ hours into my main game I still have about 1/3 of my inventory locked...It was a stupid idea.

4. Terribly designed economy which can easily be exploited to churn out hundreds of millions of currency in short periods of time, which basically devalues everything in the game since you can buy it all in no time at all.

In short, as I said, it feels like a game in beta that still needs lots of bug fixes, balancing, quality of life improvements, testing, tweaking, improving for it to feel like a polished finished game. This seems to be the trend now with game devs: release games 3-5 years too early, but collect the full purchase price now.

NMS has potential, and it is fun when you are first exploring the galaxy, but I cannot recommend it as a game. The game aspect simply isn't there. 

You collect resources and mine for ancient bones so you can sell them at a space station where you can upgrade your ship, suit and tool, and pick up quests where you have to go out into the universe and... collect resources and mine for ancient bones. 

Each outpost you find consists of the exact same scenario. You interact with a computer terminal and if you are successful you may be rewarded with nanites, which you either trade in for suit, ship or tool upgrades or you trade in for locations of additional outposts on your galactic map. 

You repeat the same cycle, over and over again, to unlock upgrades which allow you to more easily complete the cycle. Yes, it is a sandbox game, but it lacks the challenges and creative aspects of other sandbox games such as Minecraft.

Reviews.138023:
NMS is still $60, as it was at launch. You're here because you want to know if it's worth it. Well...

Let's get this out of the way: Hello Games are a small indie studio. If you're expecting the same level of polish and focus as a $60 AAA release, you will be frustrated. They aren't big enough for that and don't want to be. That being said, HG have delivered numerous DLC-sized updates at no additional cost, and plan to continue. There are no season passes or microtransactions. Your $60 buys you everything, forever.

The game is large, complex, and in a constant state of improvement. There are bugs, many of which are frustrating. So far, I haven't encountered any save-breakers, but others haven't been so lucky. Still, patches are frequent, and most of the issues I found when I started playing just a couple of months ago are gone. More than that, requested gameplay enhancements come about as often as fixes. I like the game more today than I did two weeks ago. I expect I'll like it even more next month.

The most vitriolic complaints I've seen directed at No Man's Sky, going all the way back to its launch, have been about what it isn't. NMS has never tried to be anything other than what its creators said it was: a low-key open-world exploration game. HG are committed to making the game the best it can be, but that doesn't mean it has something everyone wants. That isn't a failing of the product or its creators.

The universe of NMS is absolutely huge. Your next random jump is likely to show you something no one has ever seen before. My girlfriend and I regularly spend entire evenings just wandering or flying around random planets, or jumping aimlessly from system to system in search of new sights. If that's what you're looking for, No Man's Sky will reward you for coming back every day.

Games like Terraria, Minecraft, Satisfactory, Space Engineers - at their base value, do not have the level of depth and awe like No Man's Sky has. Endless planets to explore with an interesting story that has me coming back to it over and over and over again. I've put a lot of hours into this game in the last two week since I've purchased it - and every hour feels like an adventure. 

While the music is more reactive than anything, there are some haunting tunes you can hear that are rather beautiful, and remind me of Phillip Glass. The combat system isn't awful - as it's up to you to upgrade yourself and find what weapons and systems best fit your playstyle. Running around with the shotgun and three shields and going after the Sentinels like you've got five stars from GTA is exhillarating, even more so if you try this while in Permadeath difficulty. 

I have wept tears when I touched down on some planets that were so breath-taking and beautiful, and I definitely cried when I gathered 20 some animals on accident after throwing some bait. Gathering around me like I was the pack leader. The expressions on the NPC's and the creatures and the diversity makes me very happy to play, and I definitely have a soft spot for the Gek. 

Whatever B.S happened when No Man's Sky first dropped, it's gone. There aren't a lot of bugs save for the occasional issue with multiplayer, and sometimes being unable to complete a mission, but it's rare. I highly recommend this game, it's great fun.

Except the grind to get your first Living Ship. Really? Full-day wait times for separate items I have to literally nurse and wait on? I understand I'm literally allowing a living organism to grow to maturity, but at least let me get all the parts and pieces and THEN start the timer. Little extra unnecessary padding regarding that. And it could use a few more puzzles that allow greater rewards when exploring some planets, maybe trials for each race.

Combat trials for the Vy'keen, Brain teasers with the Korvox, and maybe some fetch quests for the Gek. I would love to see actual communities on the planets beyond just the little outposts here and there. Let some races settle down on these various planets and have families run about in little cities that have more function and shops than just the occasional trading outpost. Give the races more personality in these locations. And maybe have the ability to hire a translator as well. One of these days I'll learn all the words to all the races, but until then - wouldn't mind alternatives to understanding what these people are saying.

No Man's Sky is a very interesting game with a very interesting history. In 2016 it experienced one of the most controversial game launches in history. The product that Hello Games actually released was hardly even a shadow of all of the things it had been promised to be. There were very few features to the game beyond, "cool planet, moving on, cool planet, moving on," and almost no reason to play it for more than an hour, if even that.

Hello Games could have written No Man's Sky off as a failure and abandoned it, but they didn't. They have been releasing update after update (all free), constantly progressing the game towards what it was supposed to be in the beginning. 

Today, No Man's Sky actually does let you explore an infinite universe with your friends. Collect materials, build bases, captain your own space freighter and manage your fleet of space frigates. Fight off pirates to maintain peace, or become a pirate yourself to acquire wealth.

While the story may sometimes feel shallow, you still get to meet an interesting array of characters, from the leaders of the Nexus: Nada and Polo, to the mysterious Artemis. Even interacting with NPCs is a blast at times. Instead of installing the auto-translator device into your suit, you can interact with aliens to learn their languages yourself. What starts off as gibberish, slowly becomes clumsy understanding, and eventually perfect fluency in each dialect.

In summary, if you love space-exploration RPGs, and want to support a developer that doesn't leave a game to rot, buy No Man's Sky. I've put hundreds of hours into this game between now and launch, and each time I come back to play it after a break, I only spend more time on it. It's been worth every penny.

No Man's Sky is a game where it's primary bread and butter is space exploration and adventure. You start out crash landed on a planet and are forced to fix your ship and take to the stars. 

It's developed by Hello Games and was probably one of the worst releases of a big title of all time, however they stuck with the product and have been continually tackling the promised features list at launch and have now added most of if not all of the features it should have had at launch. This action is commendable in and of itself, and Hello Games has now set themselves up with a product that has an exceptional foundation but also one that lacks any real depth. You are still stuck doing the same several tasks over and over again with no real meaning, however, they did do many things right.

The actual exploration and adventure aspect of the game is awesome. It never gets old descending onto a planet to see what it looks like, most are unique and they range from very strange looking VR esque environments all the way to downright gorgeous planets. You can scan the plants, minerals, and animals on every planet you visit and you can actually name the system, the planets, and the plants/minerals/animals anything you want as well, so when other players run across it they can see your discoveries.

The base building is outstanding too. You can build above ground, underground, and underwater with no issues. It is intensive enough to be a decent mid game grind to build something cool, and simple enough that most everyone can make something they want between the prefabs and non prefab blocks.

The graphics are great too, they make environments look nice, ships look gorgeous in space, freighters especially.


This title SHINES in VR. It's the gold standard.


That's about where my good thoughts end however....

The stations are terribly designed. Every time you enter one you are forced to go through a forever long docking sequence, only to exit and have to walk another minute to whatever task you wish to accomplish. Want to trade? You'll need to walk a minute to the trade station from your ship. Ah darn, you realized that the only way to get inventory space is to buy it on every station you visit? Have to walk two minutes over to the merchant stalls and another minute to get back to your ship. Every station has the exact same interior, except for the ATLAS stations and the Anomaly. The ATLAS stations are about 30 seconds of docking for one to two minutes of walking for 15 seconds of story progressing dialogue. The eerie cool looks wear off extremely quickly. The Anomaly is another extreme annoyance much in the same ways the other two types of stations are, take 30 seconds to dock, a minute or more to go run to the research stalls, another minute to go get your quests, and another three to go back to the ship. This was bad enough that I actually found myself using three S class movement mods and the teleporters as much as possible just so I didn't have to endure the random "gametime fluff" of walking around on bland empty stations to accomplish simple tasks.

The on-planet sites suffer from random "game-time fluff" as much as the stations do too. Communications towers are a perfect example of this, where normally you land on the outside and have to go up three redundant ladders that don't work too well. You can try to skip them, but, youll many times get stuck on the ladder anyway. Comms towers probably wasted five minutes of my time every time I ran across one for a story mission, especially the mission where you had to repair it and it didn't tell you beforehand so you end up running up there three times because you don't know the materials you need without looking at it. There aren't many cool sites either, most of them are the same every time you see them with the exception of the inhabiting species, so running through them for a singular word for a singular species language is a bit of a drag.

This game time fluff is an extremely prevalent problem everywhere actually, it's a main reason why I went out of my way to avoid using my freighter as much as possible, even though you are basically forced to and i'll explain why. You get a freighter pretty early on and you are given a -lot- of inventory space. However, you can also dock and build a base inside of your freighter and get even more storage inside the cargo containers you can build. You can also send your frigates out on missions which are extremely rewarding. The problem with this? The route to the bridge is static, and every time you ever need to go onto your freighter for any reason, you are forced to sit through an unnecessarily long docking animation and a several minute long run to the bridge. Again encouraging you to just make a base and use the teleporter to stations and simply calling your freighter and only using it's inventory. This makes base-building inside the freighter pretty redundant unless you enjoy being bored out of your mind.

The dynamic trade system is terrible. its far too easily exploited and you can easily get infinite money by simply getting an inventory full of a material, going to a station, if they sell that material, then sell your entire stock and buy it back for 20% the price you sold it at. You can make a billion+ in a couple hours easily.

Theres also a serious lack of cool events that can happen. It would be awesome if faction wars broke out, or something meaningful happened, but, you just simply go from one procedurally generated planet to another, and once you get your fill of whatever you need, be it minerals or whatever, you spend five minutes going through random fluff that has no meaning and is only there to pad your gametime to accomplish the actual 30 seconds of meaningful task you needed to do on the station before doing it all over again. There's just too much empty, which is depressing because the foundation of what they have is absolutely terrific.

In it's current state, I would not recommend a buy off of the game by itself, objectively. However, if you do support the developers intentions of improving their game, and support their actions of not abandoning the game and continuing to release content for it, I do recommend a buy. This is a rarity in today's market and is downright commendable.

I pre-ordered the game on the initial promise of a vast single-player experience akin to many previous games of the genre. Most of that was not present in the base game, and the initial reception was suitably harsh. I put the game down in dismay, as I'd clocked too many hours for a refund by the time I realised almost none of what I was looking for could be found. 

That's changed a lot. 

Base construction, freighter ownership and modification, deeper crafting, more varied resources, storyline missions, broader trading options, and much, much more were added in during the various free updates over the past four years. Welcome changes and additions to a very flat, dull, and uninteresting game. 

I've found myself pushing back bedtime repeatedly this last week since i picked the game up again; just need to find one more recipe, or unlock another base component, earn a few more units to buy a new multitool, or upgrade another slot on my exosuit. The level of depth and scope has vastly improved. I haven't tried out the multiplayer options yet, but there seems to be quite a few new ways to play with friends in addition to the promised singleplayer experience I was originally looking for. 

For the most part, gameplay is very relaxed. You explore, scanning down new flora, fauna, and minerals. You hop from planet to planet without any loading screens in-system as you travel. You learn new words of several languages to communicate with alien species. You solve simple logic puzzles to earn new recipes or find interesting locations. That's not to say there isn't some action as combat against multiple ships can put you on the edge of your seat, and the frantic search for a few elements to recharge your environment shields can have you panicking once you realize you've used your whole stash. 

If you're looking for something outlandish, relaxing, and increasingly intricate, this may be up your alley. Plenty of mining for resources, farming, exploring, and learning interspersed with occasional moments of panic and an almost Civilization-like One-More-Turnitis. Best of luck among the stars, Traveller!

I very rarely review anything. But i'd love to share my thoughts for this game, so here goes...
I bought this game back in 2016 when it was still considered a no man's flop. After about 30 minutes i shelved the game since performance on my computer back then was very poor and, well, we all probably know the story.
but i still followed the further progress of this game's development with one eye and a few weeks ago i decided to reboot it and start a new game.
To my surprise (im using a modest laptop), performance was pretty good and the game was very well playable with the right settings, so i got started:

I woke up on a pretty mild planet and started the main quest line, found a ship and a location to build my first "base" as the main quest line asks you to do.
My first base is a small wooden "house shaped" shack. Not much bigger than a regular garden shed. I put my first portal in it and called the base "Husavik". Husavik is the name of an Icelandic town which translates to "house at a bay". my first base is also literally a house at a body of reddish water in what looks like a small canyon or crater.
Next, i was instructed to go to a space station, but i decided to take my time to fly along the planet's surface before i made my way into space. 
To my surprise, i was suddenly flying over a gigantic body of water, worthy of being called a sea or even an ocean. 
After about a minute of flying over that body of water, i saw a small island and i decided to land on it. I took a dive in the water and found that it was full of life compared to the land which had a very modest fauna and flora. I was surrounded by lots of non-hostile creatures and plants in the weirdest shapes. After abit of exploring i decided to go back out and in my ship to fly to the other side of the ocean. It took me a few more minutes to get there and i bumped into a random local trade station. I looked back and realised that my little garden shed "base" was back across that big body of water which would in reality be several hundreds of miles away.

Yes... i like this game. It's made for explorers. Its immersive and you're not in a hurry. Take your time and try to forget that its all just procedurally generated bits and bytes. Theres no competition ladder. There is no "best player". Also, you KNOW that the universe has real player characters in it. Chances that you meet up with a random other player are small, but knowing that it can actually happen makes the game environment just that little bit more "alive".
I'm curious how it will continue. Maybe new varieties of shapes for fauna and flora, boats and submarines... who knows?

Happy exploring!
Unclefester

Reviews.138379: I spent an eternity contemplating this purchase. I wasn't on board the initial hype train but was there to see it derail and fall off a bridge into a ravine. I stood by as they slowly redeemed themselves but still took little interest, until i saw the internet historian video. I had recently switched from console to PC and thought perhaps the new computing power might be able to do the game justice. I bought the game and my post purchase experience has been a microcosm of the NMS release experience. The game ran horribly when i booted it up. It looked nice but i had major frame drops and couldn't run or use the jetpack without it looking like total trash. Nothing i did in game or with NVidia helped so i was going to ask for a refund but one more google search led me to a reddit discussion about 'threads" and "cores" and editing program files. I was desperate so i tried it, and it IT COMPLETELY FIXED EVERYTHING. I am a little bothered that there hasn't been an official explanation as to why this is necessary for some people but it was an absolute game changer. I am running everything at max settings and am getting excellent FPS. The game looks absolutely stellar. It really blows me away how this hasn't been more formally addressed. All I really know in the infinite universe of No Man's Sky is that you have to go into the program files and change the number of low thread count to 0 for some people or this game runs like it has a nervous condition. This game still has then potential to be something spectacular, it might already be, but they need to address these simple performance issues before they work on anything else.

I played this game back when it first came out, and although I enjoyed it to an extent, it was incredibly repetitive and got boring quickly. It's changed a LOT since then, and I think anybody who is on the fence about purchasing it should really give it a go. I think the game is finally becoming what the developers initially wanted it to be.

After coming back to what feels like an almost completely different game, I'm almost 700 hours in, and although I've restarted a couple of times, there is hundreds of hours worth of gameplay if you enjoy exploring. There are plenty of missions, the base-building is great fun, the animals are as derpy as ever, and there's now the option to play multiplayer. On top of all this, the developers are active in improving the game and adding more and more to the game all the time. The best part, instead of releasing DLCs, all the updates are free so far!

If you're looking for something action-packed, lots of fighting etc, this isn't the game for you. This is very much a chill-out game (with a little bit of danger thrown in), very much an exploration and base-building game. The music is very pleasant, the gameplay relaxing. There are a number of different difficulty modes, including a creative mode.

Things I love about NMS:
- Endless exploring, enough variety to not get too repetitive over time.
- You can play at your own pace. Race through the missions, or explore the open universe.
- The variety of missions and the amount of stuff you can do now - from raiding depots to taking photos, fixing freighters and ships, building a base, spaceship fights and so much more.
- The nonsensical wildlife
- The Vy'keen...so adorable
- The amount of big updates and the fact that the developers seem very active

Things I don't love or would like to see in future:
- There are lots of bugs...very occasionally they can screw up your gameplay and force you to reload or start again, but this has only happened to me once or twice. Otherwise, the bugs are minor inconveniences and don't affect gameplay too badly.
- There are only three races, not including travellers. I'd love to see a couple more for variety.
- I'd also love to see more variety in the planets. There are plenty of them, and I probably haven't seen all of the rare glitched planets yet, I'm nowhere near the end of the game. I just think it'd be nice to see more biomes.
- A little more action, perhaps a couple of bad-guy NPCs, and some new horrors.
- Do something with abandoned buildings - they have so much potential but don't seem to do anything except give out nanites.
- More variety in buildings

TL;DR: Hundreds of hours of gameplay, lots and lots of things to do and frequent updates, far less repetitive than when it first came out - in fact it's almost like a brand new game. Definitely worth a buy.

Reviews.138495:
Let me be clear from the start, this game is the reason I no longer pre-order games.

Maybe even that took too long, but it is what it is. I followed this game from early on, watching its many promises at E3 2014 full of excitement because I had longed for a space-exploration game like this. Growing up a huge Star Wars and general sci-fi nerd, the possibilities seemed endless. The fully released game was a massive flop and disappointment. Most of the promised features were either missing entirely, or shadows of what was promised or even demo'd prior to the game's launch. It was incredibly ambitious from the get-go, but the developers had clearly over-promised what was realistic for their (most likely) quickly upcoming Sony-scheduled release date. The end result was a rushed game that I said would never be worth the $60 I paid for it. I played it for almost 40 hours and abandoned it.

As the first year or two went by, I would try the major updates but they were never enough to really rectify the games lack of content. I was constantly looking for other games that could do what this game promised to be, like Elite: Dangerous and the ever-in-alpha Star Citizen. Then this year, after assuming that there never could be a truly satisfying space-exploration game, I decided after another year of major updates that I would completely start a new character and try the "new" game from scratch. I have never been so wrong when I said this game would never be worth what I paid for it. 

This game has completely turned around. It has billions of explorable planets that are procedurally generated and can be anything from barren to completely stunning. The flora and fauna are all procedurally generated too and that at least makes them...interesting. I can say that they will give you a good laugh from time to time. The soundtrack matches the games aesthetic perfectly and the added story and questlines fill in much of what this game was missing. Think of this as an indie space exploration story, with minecraft like base building and exploration (endless exploration), an economy system, and endless activities. There is so much to do in this game now. I had less than 40 hours into this game before 2020. At the time of this review, I have over 4x that amount and I'm still playing it currently. The Hello Games team is still finding new ways to scratch my weird sci-fi itches with consistent updates (for free!) and is clearly dedicated to making this game into even more than it was promised to be.

Bravo Hello Games!

Great time killer, HG has done an awesome job reworking the core aspects of the game. It is currently worth every penny, and continues to receive free, and massive updates.

For those struggling with frame rates and the options menu doesn't seem to be getting the job done, here is what i did:

Navigate to: Steam\steamapps\common\No Man's Sky\Binaries\SETTINGS and open TKGRAPHICSSETTINGS.MXML with Notepad.

Inside this file, at the bottom, change: <Property name="NumHighThreads" value="#" /> to whatever your max CPU cores are. (Change the # to 6, or 8, etc)

Inside the same file, one line down, change: <Property name="NumLowThreads" value="0" />

Save and exit the file

This improved my FPS greatly, and i was able to then turn my options settings up beyond low specs and have a smooth game play experience

Enjoy!

This game had come a very long way since its original release and represents one of the very few redemption stories in the gaming industry. Nobody can deny that the original release was overhyped, unfinished and broken, but unlike the was majority of developers these days Hello Games stuck in, finished the game, and improved it far beyond of what had been originially promised. All that without paid expansions, DLCs, microtransactions and the like. Sometimes I wonder how they can even keep the lights on, but in reality this is just how big publishers want us to think. Hello Games is a studio of about 25 people who make a game they care about and it shows.

A few years ago I would've said that NMS lacks the polish and QA of a typical $60 tripple-A release, but these days it is the other way around. NMS can by no metric be called bug-free, but it is drastically less so than a typical Bethesda game, and unlike those, bugs are actually getting fixed quite fast, considering the size of the team.

Overall, expect a chill exploration and stuff-gathering experience with pretty sights on the way. The story is interesting and weird, if a bit janky in execution, but even more charming for it, like watching someone's first theatrical play.

Personally, I feel the game is well optimized, a game where I can fly into space, onto a massive planet, space again, and onto ANOTHER massive planet has no reason to be running as smoothly as it does. My computer is nearly five years old and it runs like a charm.

Lets start with what's good about the game. The game has wonderful atmosphere, it honestly makes you feel like there's a whole universe with endless exploration and possibilities. The language system, trading system, and the buildings you find on a planet just overall make you feel like you're a Galatic Traveler, I would say it's unrivaled in any game thus far.

The game itself is calm, almost zen like, gives you the same old relaxing feel as Minecraft. Base building on many different planets, going from place to place, and overall exploring is a perfect medium of relaxing and interesting without being dreadfully boring.

However, the game doesn't exactly give you a lot of hand holding when it comes to certain aspects that feel pretty important, yet the tutorial is fairly long for anybody's taste. Some things could've been streamlined, mentioned off-hand, or discovered by oneself. Anybody with 1/4th of a brain could've figured out how to find fly from a Planet to a Space Station if you already showed them how to fly to a Planet. But nobody is going to guess off-hand that pressing Q-E while trying to upgrade a Exosuit Inventory Slot will allow you to upgrade a Technology Slot which you can get by going to a terminal NEXT to the Merchant and not the Merchant Themself, or that you can only learn certain crafting Blueprints you need to progress from Abandoned Facilities you'll find random on planets.

Additionally, The game does feel incredibly slow, and having to get Oxygen to refill your Life-Support, Sodium for you Hazardous Environment Protections, Carbon for your Mining Beams, Di-hydrogen for your Launch Thrusters...blah blah blah. It's not really an engaging aspect, it's the equivalent of a Hunger or Thirst meter in any other Survival Game but it doesn't feel fun. It's just a second of my time wasted to open the menu and refill it. But it doesn't become a problem later on in the game as the resources you need come in abundance anyway. 

And movement is also INCREDIBLY slow even when you can sprint AND you're given a jetpack, it still takes forever to get to Point A to Point B by foot. Luckily there's a trick where if you sprint, melee attack (Q) and then activate your jetpack it catapults you forward (a trick I just call thrusting) without that it'd be borderline unplayable as you move slower than a stick of butter up-hill.

Another aspect of the game many players can't stand are the sentinels, a bunch of floating robots that get nettled when you attempt to "alter the planet in anyway". It's a good story concept, but yeesh does it make me want to headbutt a beltsander sometimes. Imagine playing Minecraft but every once in awhile a GTA Cop will pass by and beat the crap out of you if you try and play the game. 

If you trigger a sentinel you either have to high-tail it or kill it. Whatever, smash a robots face in, no biggie. But once you kill one, you get a star and wave after wave of sentinels come with progressively bigger and badder sentinels. And the spoiled cherry on top this egg-shelled filled cake is THEY DO NOT STOP. They continue on and on until you high tail out of there. It's just ludicrous and annoying to get pegged by a damn flying eyeball with a water-pistol and having to run from it just because you don't feel like wasting your time.

Despite those two aspects, the game overall grants a fair bit of enjoyment, I'd say it definitely gives it's money's worth for the amount of time you can suck into this game. If you enjoy survival and base-building games but don't feel like getting shot in the back of the head by a six year-old. I recommend this game, but if you like higher octane games, this may be too slow for you.

Firstly, if you're tossing up whether to purchase this game, look up The Engoodening of No Man's Sky on YT by Internet Historian. He will give you the full story and explain exactly why YOU SHOULD BUY THIS GAME (possibly again for many people)! 

***A  comment on the devs***
The developers deserve HUGE props for turning this disaster of a game into something even more than it was ever first envisioned. They have released free update after free update towards making this game as amazing as it currently is. Right now, Living Ships!!! Hello Games could have taken my money and run as I was one of the many who have followed the game since the beginning. But unlike many others, I never entirely gave up hope on this game. Thankfully, the dev team knuckled down and continued to push through the hate they received and pulled possibly the gaming industries biggest 180 degree turn for the better. 

This game and it's developers will go down in history as two things. First, the worst way to hype up a game and release it. Second, the best way to stay loyal to your player base and make amends. Actions speak louder than words and Hello Games are pumping out free DLC after free DLC and only continue to engage with the community, fix and enhance the game and just all round be what good developers should be. They've made the worst mistakes, learned from them and become one of the best developers competing with AAA titles as an indie dev team. They have my upmost respect.

***The Game***
Do you like space games? Do you like exploration? Do you like simple yet effective game systems and mechanics that are mostly intuitive to understand but still give the game a sense of depth in learning and understanding? Do you like playing with friends but also being able to progress alone when they're not around? I've found all of this and more to be offered by the current updates of NMS. From running around doing missions with mates, to simply grinding resources while listening to music after a long week of work. It's both fun and thrilling, but can also be therapeutic and peaceful. I've enjoyed the game so much that I even bought the game on PS4 which I take with me when I travel to see family on holidays etc. Despite running two different characters on two different platforms, I equally enjoy the experience on both. Sure there are still bugs from time to time as with any game, but with how consistently the devs have been updating the game, they tend to eliminate bugs quite quickly. The environments no longer feel as empty as they did on release and I actively enjoy wizzing around on a planet looking for different points of interest and even that's helped by being able to exchange planetary charts at space stations. Being able to build a base to call home but also being able to visit and explore other impressive bases is fantastic and inspirational and the community is pretty great for helping one another out, especially for community events and challenges. Overall, the game is bloody well worth the money, ESPECIALLY when it's on sale which I often see it for 50% off. In Australia where games are always hella expensive, you'll see it down to $42 with a 50% off sale. I'd easily pay $60+ for the game in it's current state so I'm quite happy I kept my copy from when I originally bought it on release all those years ago. This game currently sits as one of my favourite games in my steam library.

Ill Start by making my point simple then i will break it down for those who would like some explanation..

-If you play video games to overcome challenges and obstacles with fun and interesting mechanics, a compelling story, and reward for your competence, then this game is probably not for you.

-If you like to role play, then this game might be for you.

I do not think I have ever played a game with as much potential as No Man's Sky, but there is a reason this game is still poorly rated, given that all you hear about it these days is how the game has achieved some form of glory and redemption, but in reality, this game is so boring that i cant compare it to anything other than a virtual tour. There seems to be ZERO point to anything you do as all you will be doing is grinding to become more efficient, so you can grind some more. Add some travelling and you have NMS game play loop in its entirety, and it is all very easy, even when you first start out, because little to nothing will hinder your ability to do the only thing this game really has to offer, GRIND. The only "challenge" this game offers is managing your inventory. There is NO risk/reward factor, and the only time you ever really feel good about anything you have done in this game is when you build a sweet base, but that is basically ALL there is, unless you want to explore the overwhelming number of procedurally generated planets. Which I will say can be beautiful and cool looking from time to time, but that sense of beauty and coolness will wear off fast, then your back to the game play loop of grinding just to sight see, and grind some more. This game is entirely too based around being JUST a sandbox, and because of this, you have to make up your own fun too a degree iv never experienced in a game before. Even a game as similar and simple as Minecraft has challenge and reward. Why do non of these updates for NMS address the only real problem this game has suffered from since day 1? Without meaning, without risk, without reward, without challenge, this game is just not entertaining for most people.
