It definitely struggles with keeping the gameplay fresh and exciting, which I think is mostly due to dumping almost all of it's features on you at once, becoming overwhelming at the start and underwhelming later on.

Still, your first time getting in your ship and leaving the planet you originally spawned on, never to return again is like nothing else! 

It's a difficult game to recommend as it's not really like any other game. if you're unsure I suggest waiting for a sale as you'll either love it, or find it incredibly dull.

Reviews.139044:
[h1] It's time to forget the past! [/h1]

[b] Not sure if you want to buy No Man's Sky? Read this! [/b]

If you were to tell me 3 and a half years ago that Hello Games would continue to work on this game and eventually create a universe unmatched by any of it's rivals and competitors, I honestly wouldn't have believed you. The amount of lies we were given was countless, the amout of bugs we got was unfathomable, and the amount of false hype for a game with bare-minimun gameplay footage was, and still is, unmatched. I often wonder how people can knowingly lie to other people, even though they know the truth. This still baffles me and I haven't forgiven Sean for what he did, but atleast I can understand it to a certain extent. But I'm not making this review to complain;

Here we have, at the start of 2020, a beautiful open world survival space adventure game with a huge playerbase. A playerbase that never stops liking the game and always comes back for new updates and content-drops. There has been a total of 8 major updates; Foundation, Pathfinder, Atlas Rises, NEXT, The Abyss, Visions, the 2.0 BEYOND update and Synthesis. all of which contains a TON of content.

The reason I write this review today is because I want to praise Hello Games. I want to plaise them because they came out with a new update yesterday, [i]Living Ships[/i]. This is the newest major update, making it a total of 9 major updates and it certainly looks good. I'm eager to try it, but this came as a shock to me. I thought the Synthesis update would be the last for this game, but i guess not. In the "No Man's Sky Living Ship Update" Steam post they put out yesterday (19th february 2020) Hello Games talks about how they will continue to provide more updates for the game, and this gives me hope. It gives me a hope that Hello Games might be the one to lead this generation of games into the future and show other developers and AAA companies how it's done! 

"[i]How can you say so much about a game you've only played for 17 hours?[/i]"
Good point, but what my steam page doesn't say is that I used to only play PS4. That brings me to another point, the game is super well optimized for every console. It might not be 60fps all the time, but the tear or lag is never too much to handle. 

As i'm writing this I'm slowly realizing that this won't be a review after all. It might just be me who wants to let the gaming community know that Hello Games is working their asses of to make up for their mistakes. I used to hate on this game, but I'm am also one of the millions of people who pre-ordered it. I never refunded the game, and every time I heard that No Man's Sky was getting updates, I would slowly become more and more intrigued. At one point i just downloaded the game back onto my PS4 and played the shit out of it! I had soo much fun! The visuals, aesthetics, sound quality, epicness, gameplay and controls just felt perfect, exactly like eating a perfectly rolled burrito with all of your favorite ingredients.

I'm really bad at convincing people to try new games, but I usually don't write this much for a single game. If anyone reads this; I hope you try this game and like it! It's 50% of steam as of today, but it's worth every penny!

Reviews.139128: There are approx 200,000 million trillion stars in our universe. Meanwhile in No Man's Sky, there are approx 473,025 billion stars. In other words, No Man's Sky covers 2.365125e-9 of our universe's stars. That's 0.0000000002365125, which is quite a lot. No Man's Sky is the only game in which it makes any sense to draw this kind of comparisons. It is also the only game in which the size of the game world eludes my grasp. I cannot comprehend it, and that's what I love about it. The way this is achieved is rather simple, every new solar system is a variation on the same set of parameters that determine the number of planets, their geology, moons, as well as the economy, etc. In effect, traveling through this universe, you just keep reshuffling the parameters of one solar system-sized game world. However, the illusion works as long as it is able to keep surprising you. The illusion makes you feel that No Man's Sky is not just a game, but a universe simulator. Once the campaign ends, you will likely have seen a big chunk of what NMS has to offer, but with the recent updates, there is potential to continue enjoying this magical sandbox indefinitely.

Reviews.139203:
Did this game have a rocky launch way back when? Yea. But that's what happens when a studio gets flooded and Sony helps you out. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Short Version: 
The game is amazing with a decent to wonderful narrative and Hello Games are constantly updating it. If you watch the developer twitter and they post an emoji, a large update is inbound so watch out, it's a-comin'. I just wish there was more customization options for ships and freighters but those may be an update at one point. All in all; Playing this game in VR is a dream come true!

Long Version:
PROS: The game's story is really well written and has a point to it. Almost like multiple Star Trek episode that discusses issues about -kzzkt- and -kzzkt- (spoilers, I know). You can play this game passively, taking the high road, focusing on exploration, or mining, or you can be the very thing you seek to destroy and steal from freighters. With an infinite game, there are infinite possibilities. 

Hello Games is constantly updating the game with new features, items, cosmetics, and fun new story and side objectives. They always want to add more and seem to always listen to the community. For the constant desire to be connected with their fan/user base, that is worth the game alone.

What can you do in No Man's Sky? You can explore, index, and colonize new planets, systems and galaxies. You can learn the native languages of the species in the universe. You can be a pirate if you feel like it and attack freighters or be the one to defend them. You can build bases or own a freighter to call home. Oh, and did I mention you can do it all in VR as well? Holy heck the VR is nice. It's not perfect, but they're always touching it up in whatever way they can. I just hope they fix the "out of play area" nonsense for players like me who use large play-areas and like to physically move around. 

CONS (note, these aren't really cons): If I have to nit-pick, I do have a few personal cons, but these are things I can see being added in a new update sooner or later, so take them or leave them. But it has to do with customization. 

1: First tuft of customization is the Star Ships. I wish that the exotics like the Squid or the fancy royal one (blanking the name at the moment) had different interiors than the default round cockpit. While that's my favorite cockpit, I feel it isn't fitting for these "Exotic Ships". The newest exotic ship, the -kzzkt-, is completely unique, inside and out and I can't wait to get one, so it seems they want to move that direction. 

2: Freighter customization! Not talking about the amount of slots, I feel like those are fine. The inside of a freighter is my focus here. The area of construction is 21x21 and you can have 13 decks. That's a lot of space, however, what I really want to do is hollow out sections so I can have balcony areas of the ship to give two levels in some parts. (My friend and I really wanna make Tarok Nor). Another feature I'd love to have is using more base components in your freighter. Finally, I love being able to change the interior color of the freighter, but I'd like to change the theme. The bridge and the walls all look exactly the same and should represent the species that control it.

2b: I want to fly my freighter with a group of friends like it's Star Trek Bridge Crew, Pulsar, or Guns of Icarus. That would make NMS a 10 out of 10 for me, hands down. 

3: When I learn a new word, I want an easy way to see what the word I learned meant in reference through my in-game catalogue. 

All-in-all, I recommend this game for anyone wanting a VR experience or a fun new space exploration title with rich and layered lore. 

I hope this -kzzkt- review helps new travelers on their -kzzkt- journey.

Reviews.139227:
Every couple of years I get bit by the minecraft bug and feel like going into an epic journey of discovery and survival. Unfortunately minecraft survival mode was the only option (in 3d) till this game came around. If you asked me to recommend this game a few years back, I would have to say no. It was a disappointment at launch, the coding that was rendering the world was complex but its output was rather simple resulting in simplistic looking tacky environments and creatures but with nothing really to do but to mine for minerals to travel to the center but there was potential. Potential that Hello Games Silently chipped away, polishing and refining the game over the years. As it stands now, it is definitely worth endorsing. If you are someone who was into minecraft or any other similar crafting heavy game, then this will compliment you well. Although not quite as deep (its still getting there), there is a wealth of content that the developers have added overtime that will allow you spend hours jumping from planets to planets and galaxies alike. 

The premise is simple, you have crash landed on an alien planet at the edge of the galaxy and must find mine resources to repair your suit and ship must travel towards the center of the galaxy. Someone or something has been leaving you crumbs of tech forever leading you deeper into the center. 

At the start the game will ask you a few choices. Like Minecraft there is a survival mode and a creation mode that basically allows you to do whatever you want. The Survival mode is the main highlight for those that want more of a game than a creation tool. 

Pros: If you get past the initial grind, there is a deep sense of mystery and discovery that Hello Games have managed to layer onto the initially simplistic template. Following the main mission objectives reward with more possibilities to create and explore the vast galaxies that are randomly generated. 

The graphics in this game has definitely come along way. Landscapes look beautiful at different times of the day, even dead planets and deserts look beautiful with improved textures and shadow mappings. As you explore you will see more planets variety that can range from ordinary to bat shit weird and everything in between. NPCs look less cartoonish and there is a good bit of variety between random creatures of the same species. 

The game does have a multiplayer setting which you can set to have people randomly drop into your game at any point. There is also a multiplayer hub where you will see other players run around. You can team up and complete mission objectives that reward you with exotic currencies for cosmetics and items that can further upgrade your existing tech. 

Secondary missions further add more incentives to explore and discover items and recipes that further expand your base and weaponry. If you spend time investing in some of these you can eventually start owning multiple ships a frigate and even a car to help expedite the tedium of jogging on foot. 

Ship combat can feel quite satisfying. Owning several variety of top tier ships in a frigate can be an appealing prospect for an expanding base armada. 

There is more that is yet to be discovered and there will be more added to the game over time. NMS is a living game where the developers each year seem to add more depth to the large universe they have created. Expect the game to get more complicated as time goes on.

Cons: The initial grind can be an overwhelming brick wall that can put off many. Constantly managing your suits environmental protection units can feel like a chore initially. 

Graphics have been overhauled but is far from perfect. Its an unfortunate but expected issues with larger games where everything cannot be accounted for. Make sure your PC's CPU is capable of generating large bodies of mass and water. The game is no longer simple and as such requires more power than it did a year or two ago. Expect this requirement to increase with in a few more updates time.

Multiplayer exist but is still a bit rough around the edges. Opening game up to random travellers can bring grief but there are options to counter that. Expect trolls guarding the end point of the weekly missions to prevent you from completing it. Make sure player damage is off. The extent of muckery an errant troll can do on another's world is unknown. 

The secondary missions are simplistic at best. Infact the whole mission structure of the game is rather simple point A to B sort of deal. But there are several types of these that are layered on top of each other to give it some depth. There isn't too much variety between them all unfortunately but the lust for a useful recipe makes the grind worthwhile. 

Ship controls can feel a bit awkward but combat on foot is at minimum at best. This game is not a shooter and combat is a means to survive in most cases. 

The game keeps expanding but hasn't quite yet reached the point where a full tag of $60 is fair asking price. Currently at the time of this writing there is an offer on steam for $30 which is currently the recommended price for this game. 

Conclusion: The game has come a long way and deserves the praise it is getting but it is still still growing. It being a living game that is continually update definitely makes it a game to keep revisiting. It has become my staple way of taking a break in between AAA games.

Honestly, If you're comparing the game from the beginning of its lifespan to what it is today, it's literally two different games. Hello Games really has out done themselves when it comes to the updated content that has been released over the span of three years. It's a bonus in my opinion that the content updates are also free verses some other games (like Ark or Conan Exiles for example) that you have to pay for updated content. 

If you enjoy the sense of exploration, base building, and shooting at things then seriously try this game out. At the moment, I have over 500 hours played and I'm still entertained on things to do. There are a plethora of systems and galaxies to explore and discover. When it comes to the multiplayer aspect, its improved quite a bit - especially from the beginning of the game. You can still play in a party with your friends and enjoy what the game has to offer. There is also the option to also meet new travelers, do actual party missions, and a lot more. The base building has gotten a lot better too! You can build from as low as the ocean depths to now as high as the sky (literally floating bases are pretty neat). Really, the only limit when it comes to building in this game is your imagination. The combat alone is pretty entertaining. You have a few options on how you want to set up your personal style (from throwing grenades to shooting laser beams) with both multi tool and your ship. Also, if you wanted to become a space pirate, you have that option too lol. The story not only has changed a bit from beginning of the game to the beyond update but now its different. You don't have to jump around like crazy anymore while being confused with the story. As you progress and follow the missions for the story, it will not only make more sense to the places that you travel, but the story line itself is more intriguing. 

Overall, If you're still thinking on giving this game a try, you won't regret it. This game truly has become one of my absolute favorites. I hope this review helps a bit. Until then, happy gaming and happy exploring traveler!

This game is a lot of fun for the first dozen hours or so. You craft a few things, meet some aliens at a weird space station, land on half a dozen planets and meet some weird creatures and see remote outposts/wrecks.  But then you go to your second solar system and see the same space station (just a different shape), the same planets (just a different colour), the same aliens (there are only 3 types), and the same creatures (this one has a longer neck) and the same remote outposts (this one staffed differently) and the same wrecks. Solar system number three is more or less the same, and guess what you'll see at number four?!

So with all this repetition, the game relies on its story missions and base building elements to keep it different and to make it feel like you're actually making progress. But each of these is bogged down in so much resource gathering that everything is so unnecessarily drawn out to take as long as possible. Every upgrade to your suit/ship/multi-tool requires parts, the parts have to be crafted from material which you have to gather from from many different locations. These have to be put in a portable refiner that in turns needs material collected before it can be built and more material to power it. This coupled with the fact that you have a tiny inventory that is tedious to expand, means it feels like a lot of "busy-work" to keep the player busy and make it feel like value for money when you see how many hours you've pumped into it.

The game is gorgeous to look at and although I've not been around to see the previous versions of it, the NMS community are full of praise at how much progress has been made since a disastrous launch. If you have the patience of a saint and love resource gathering at it's fullest you have a hell of a game to play. I can't get along with the basic workings of it though and will call it a day.

original review:

it is incredibly frustrating how broken this game still is even after they've been fixing it for over two years after its initial release...

but then again have they been fixing it or did they just try to cram everything (co-op, ship to ship combat, vehicles etc. etc.) they promised before launch into the game to "make it better"?

-quest markers bug out
-quest givers disappear so you cant hand in completed quests
-sometimes quests don't advance because it doesnt register you've already done the thing (it somehow missed me warping to another system but then registered it when i jumped back to where i came from)
-markers in general are more of a suggestion than actual facts and since they are the only thing you have to orientate yourself, this can be quite frustrating. sometimes they just vanish when you get close, sometimes they split and you have two from the same quest... one that leads you nowhere and one that disappears too when you get close.
-markers to stuff you would want to find again (buildings, ports etc.) disappear, while markers for stuff you already discovered (e.g. those ancient stones) stay, so you visit them over and over which is frustrating too because you can only interact with them once.
-you have no map aside from the starfield map, so your only option to orientate yourself on a planet/moon is one single point of interest you can set yourself
-enemy ai is basically non-existent, ancient horror can just be avoided by jumping on a roof and these drones are more of a nuisance than anything else

-teleportation is disabled at start and is then enabled at some point (without the game even telling me about it) for no apparent reason...

and yet this is a unique and fascinating adventure game that feels like it wants to be so much more. it is still apparent how they overpromised and underdelivered and that's really a shame, i feel it could be a lot better if it was just a little more focused, instead they tried to make it everything...

if they really wanted to do this game a solid, start by fixing some of the fundamentals first and stop adding more stuff until the base experience is well rounded.

would i recommend this game? oof... thats a tough one. if you think you'd like a space exploration game thats unlike anything else out there and can forgive its bugs and glitches (which definitely marred the experience for me) - go for it! otherwise maybe wait two more years...

i'd prolly rate it neutral if i could

Reviews.159734:
Now before I get in to the meat of my review, I need to get a few key points and a little bit of history out of the way first to begin with. 

These points are regarding the disastrous 2016 launch, and the issues that contributed to it and its ultimate culmination. One could imagine that the game was ill fated from the beginning. 

• During development in 2014, Hello Games' studio was subject to a flood which pretty much destroyed all of their equipment.
• Hello Games was embattled in a trademark dispute with British Sky Broadcasting, the UK cable TV arm of Rupert Murdoch's utter scumbag media empire over the use of the word 'sky'.
• Sean Murray's naivety and inexperience when being interviewed by the press. There's no denying that he said some things that he perhaps shouldn't have said.
• The pre-release trailers not being clearly marked with a disclaimer stating that what was shown was subject to change and was not representative of the final product.
• The pre-release hype being escalated to almost unbelievable proportions by the fanbase. 
• The 2016 launch edition should have released as a tech demo under an early access/beta model. However, despite all of the previous setbacks; Sony, wanted to rush it out of the door for their flagship PS4 console. 
• Bad gameplay principles, mechanics or design that Hello Games perhaps thought worked in their heads but in reality did not.
• A lot of people thought it was bad form for Hello Games to charge £40 for an incomplete product, I don't blame them. They at least didn't charge £60.
• The death threats that Sean Murray and the Hello Games team were receiving were both inexcusable and reprehensible. 

In stark contrast, however:

• Hello Games' current studio is in an elevated position and on an incline and is no longer at immediate risk of future flooding.
• Sean Murray's negative experiences from the 2016 launch and over what was said in interviews prior to launch have without a doubt made him a much, much better person.
• Hello Games have since reversed a lot of gameplay principles, mechanics or design that initially simply didn't work.
• Hello Games paid it forward by sticking with their dream project and not letting it die on arrival. They could have just as easily taken the money and ran. They didn't. Yet the blind rage and toxicity continued. Had this been EA, Activision, or Ubisoft, nobody would have batted an eye, it would have just been acknowledged as standard operating procedure. 
• Hello Games have since pushed out TEN. FREE. UPDATES. Three of which are major content updates, and also including VR. If this was the likes of EA, Activision or Ubisoft, you'd be paying for each of these through the nose.
• Hello Games uphold themselves to a much higher standard than some of the other AAA developers out there, especially those that churn out mass produced yearly cash grabs.

Lastly:

• 3 years is an impressive turnaround time for a project that was initially believed to be dead on arrival.
• Hello Games have without a doubt, earned the reputation of being an underdog or dark horse in the AAA video game industry, and rightly so.
• No Man's Sky is without a doubt, an astounding technical achievement from both a software engineering and a mathematics standpoint. Yet both the game and the team still gets shit on regularly for what happened in 2016. If you are one of these people, have you any idea how difficult game development is? Particularly for a game of this nature, scope, and ambition? Honestly, it's time to let go. It's time to stop.
• Sean Murray's initial 4 person team for No Man's Sky must have either been child prodigies in their youth, or had very, very, very, very good maths tutors. It's also plainly obvious that they are complete geeks and their social skills have suffered as a result making them introverts, and as such they don't do speaking to the public very well. However, Sean's public speaking skills have vastly improved since 2016.
• No Man's Sky is absolutely not for everyone. If you find that what it has to offer is not for you, you are within your rights to request a refund.
• No Man's Sky continues to receive ongoing support and content updates.

And now on to the review:

No Man's Sky is a slow-burn, niche, procedurally generated space exploration sandbox that explores the themes of existentialism in its main story arc and also goes out of its way in making you feel like a stranger in a strange land, with a strong emphasis on seeing planets and creatures that no one else has seen before. In short, it can be described as Minecraft but in space.

Both the visuals and the audio are absolutely stellar (pardon the pun). The art style is intended to resemble that of retro sci-fi book covers from the 1970s. The sound effects are satisfying. The ambient background music/soundtrack is sublime and is composed by Sheffield post rock band 65daysofstatic, it has to be heard to be believed. Be sure to have the volume up when you dock at the first space station.

Gameplay is broad and varied enough to suit many gameplay styles such as low key role-play, looter shooter, racing, exploration, and construction; with multiplayer being entirely optional. Multiplayer in this game is more oriented towards cooperative play as opposed to full PVP. If you are looking for PVP in the vein of Elite Dangerous or EVE Online, then unfortunately this game is probably not for you. Some gameplay loops are still not quiet perfect and still have their issues, so expect these to be reworked in the future. Unique features include making food in order to impress an alien Gordon Ramsay, making music, and growing your very own biological starship from an alien egg.

Multiplayer interactions are centred around a social hub called the Space Anomaly that can be called in to any star system. In the Space Anomaly, you can form a squad of up to 4 players to undertake and complete cooperative missions. There are also special types of missions which reward valuable items or currency for even more exotic items, these include time limited missions that are available once a day and once every weekend.

In order to 'make it' in this universe, you're going to need to not just get a grasp of most of the gameplay mechanics, but also get to know the natives and how they think and what they feel. You will also need to build up your reputation among the intelligent races by learning about their customs, their languages, solving their problems, and exercising careful diplomacy. 

You will also need to mine, manufacture and trade goods to make bank enough to be able to afford the very best starship, technology and equipment. To assist in this, you can set down on any planet and establish a remote habitable outpost there, followed by hooking it up to an energy supply before you can commence planet-side operations. Your non-portable devices and technology will also need to be connected to the power grid before they can work. You can also hire and assign research assistants to your outpost, who will help you unlock new technology or product crafting recipes, including but not limited to terrestrial vehicles. 

You will also want to catalogue undiscovered planets, species of creatures, plants, flowers, bushes and trees as you will be rewarded for doing so. Be warned though, as not every planet is hospitable or welcoming of you presence. Some planets are simply too hot or too cold, while other planets have face melting levels of toxicity or ionising radiation. Some planets experience raging storms, while on other planets you may not be the top of the food chain, as local predatory species may want to chow down on you for lunch. Lastly, the delicate ecosystems of most planets are protected by a horde of self-replicating autonomous police drones that will go terminator on your ass if you harvest resources too aggressively. Both 'Goldilocks' and truly weird planets do exist, but they are generally uncommon enough to incentivise exploration.

No Man's Sky gets a lot of hate for not living up to the hype.
I didn't participate in the hype. I ignored it as best I could. After it came out, I waited a good long while to pick it up cheap.
This is a great game. Maybe it's not what some people expected, but it's exactly what I always wanted. Let me explain:

Once upon a time, a genius named Will Wright built a career on amazing games like SimCity, SimAnt, SimEarth, SimCopter, and yeah, The Sims.

One day, he is interviewed by TIME Magazine, and talks about this game he's working on called SPORE. The description was magical, and one young boy knew this would be the perfect game.
Years pass, but that boy never gave up hope that SPORE would come, and then finally, it did. He'd downloaded the free Creature Creator demo, and knew his little laptop wouldn't be able to handle the full game, so he decided to build his own PC first. A year later, he'd saved up enough money to build a serious gaming PC, and it was glorious.

Then, he bought SPORE, rushed home, and installed it.

And it was great! Not quite as deep and complex as the boy had expected, but it was a lot of fun.
In a single afternoon, he'd reached the much-anticipated Space Stage and could fly around a procedural galaxy.
...and then he got bored.
There were other problems with SPORE that the boy could see as his enthusiasm for life cracked and slowly fell away, but the most notable problem was the simple lack of fun in the Space Stage.

Years later, this boy was a man who still bore the puffy, itchy scars of SPORE's let-down. He had a chance to get No Man's Sky cheap, so he did. As he played, the game seemed oddly comforting and vaguely familiar. After a few hours, he finally understood why.

No Man's Sky is what the end of SPORE should have been.

10/10 Greatest childhood disappointment finally resolved.

UPDATE:
There's been a few big updates since my review, and I've played over 90 hours since. So far, this game keeps getting better! Quality-of-life improvements like backpack refiners reduce the grind, while the new space content has really brought interstellar exploration to new heights. If every game studio worked so hard to keep refining their games, the industry would be better off.

Over 3 years down the road this game got measurably better!

It's still maybe only a quarter of a $60 game, but it's an adequate $20 indie game now.

But even with all the improvements that happened, I can still play it only as a walking simulator with a few other things added on. Approaching it from any other angle simply causes me too much frustration:

* UI design is completely lacking. There is no central guideline for how a player is supposed to interact with the game world. For the life of me I cannot remember in which quick menu I have to use D-pad for navigation, in which - right trigger and in which - A button.

* Adding to the previous point, UI is full of sharp edges that kick you right in the stomach for no reason. Want to hand in a mission to a space station NPC? Sure, but now you have to stare blankly at that NPC for 3 seconds while we show you notifications in top right corner. Want to warp to another system to mine some cadmium? Haha, loser, now sit through 10 full seconds of us showing you where the next Atlas interface is without being able to do anything about it.

* With Beyond inventory system got better - you can now hold up to 9999 items in one slot instead of 250. But you still do run into "inventory full" quite often, simply because you need to pick up many kinds of stuff in order to make something. And you still have to juggle items across 2 to 6 separate inventories.

* For trying to play it as an exploration game - it's way too repetitive. Groups of structures are the same on all planets. Minerals quite often look the same on different planets and just have different names so you have to scan them again. After maybe an hour you've seen it all.

And aside from that, performance is not great. On GTX 1060 it struggles to maintain 60fps@1080p on mininal settings (called "Standard" in-game).

P.S.: I've seen positive reviews claiming that this game is easy to play while stoned. I can kinda see how it can work nicely with that, so, yeah, maybe try that.

The game could be great and if you don't play VR or leave the Euclid galaxy, you'll have no issue. However, if you play VR, it doesn't implement all of the features despite tham saying as much (what's new, right?).

Here is a small subset of bugs/missing features that I have reported. I've probably reported 50 bugs and only 5 or so have been fixed. I've attempted to follow up on my reports but have never received a reply from Hello Games.

-VR players can't use the camera mode. So all those capture an image missions from mission vendors are worthless. If you abandon them, you lose rank. So you're just stuck with a bunch of missions that you can't even do.

-VR players can't ride creatures.

-VR players can rename anything.

-Driving an Exocraft in VR is broken. Often times the wheel gets ripped out your hands.

-In VR every now and then, the grab position on the joystick is reset, making it difficult to deal with when in space fights.

-No build camera in VR

-Multitool models are ~66% the size of the displayed tool when equipped.

-VR hands are at the wrong offset.

-Can't see galaxy center in VR when in the galaxy map. You also move really slow in the galaxy map in VR so when you have max jump range, it takes a couple minutes to find your max destination when free exploring.

-If you leave the Euclid galaxy and return via base teleportation, your teleport list will only list bases and systems in the new galaxy.

-All planets that have an atmosphere have storms every couple of minutes so just wondering around a beautiful planets isn't even relaxing.

No Man's Sky has become an amazing immersive and fun experience, a far cry from its original outing. I, like many, was among the thousands who were unimpressed with the product at launch. With seamless multiplayer, an endearing single player story, and enticing hypnotic gameplay loop, NMS has found it's footing in the sandbox multiplayer genre. I have left my review from those years back underneath this update to show just how far Hello Games has brought NMS. Truly astounding in this day and age to see a developer stick to a project after being so publicly chastised, kudos.

-------------------------------------------------------------------
Below is my original review of No Man's Sky as of launch 2016:
[[Unfortunately one of my most anticipated games of the year has fallen flat on its face. No Man's Sky, while on the surface seems like everything you could want in a science fiction survival game, cannot even seem to pull the player out of the same habits hour after grueling hour. In this game the premise is to inevitably reach the center of the galaxy if you can be bothered. Admittedly the first few hours were engaging, mostly because the lack of a tutorial means that you are forced to learn everything as it comes at you, but once you understand the mechanics this game becomes a long droll to the galactic core.

Content aside, the technical issues with this game are absurd. You are locked into 30 FOV with no way to increase. The terrain has a mind boggling amount of pop in, meaning that even though a planet looks cool from space it can still be garbage once you land. Your ship is cluncky and feels like an auto pilot takes the wheel from you when you do something dangerous. "oh? You wanted to fly through that canyon? how about we fly over it instead?"

I was so excited for this game, but it seems like sony has gimped it for the sake of ps4 players and Hello Games has just given PC players the most lackluster port imaginable. I wish I wasnt as excited for this game now, I wish Hello Games delivered on their promises. I wish a lot of things but mostly that I could get my money back.]]

-space battles are a joke. every once in a while two ships will attack you, and sometimes when you come out of hyperspace there is 10-20 ships attacking a freighter. that's it. those are the only two scenarios I've ever encountered. 

-alien "factions" are just a few different types of various aliens, never interacting with each other, or even doing really anything at all other than standing in one place. the only difference is if you are in good standing with them, they might recharge your shield or give you a weapon worse than the one you already have. 

-THERE IS LITERALLY NOTHING TO DO. you find a new planet, you land, you gather some resources, learn some words, see a variation of the same fucking alien standing in the same fucking place, and that's it. You leave, you find a new planet, and do the same thing, ALL OVER AGAIN. 18 quintillion times, apparently. 

-the menu system is abysmal. just an all around terrible design. no hot keys, no short cuts, just an endless struggle to gain more inventory slots. that's basically the entire point of the game. gain more inventory slots.

all in all, I have been following this games development for over a year, tried my very hardest to not get my expectations too high, made the decision to purchase the game despite the negative feed back, and now if I don't seem some free DLC that adds some ACTUAL SUBSTANCE -- I don't know if I will ever buy another game from this developer as long as I live. 



quite frankly, I'm genuinely insulted, and feel very foolish. sad face emoji.

**Update 4 Years Later**

The updated game actually rocks now.  It's very in-depth and now it seems like there is too much content to maintain and enjoy.  Kudos to you, Hello Games, for making good with your promises.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I know that I am not the first one to mention being disappointed in this game, but I wanted to give my honest opinion and hopefully it will help someone somewhere out there.  

I should qualify that thumbs down on recommendation; I wish there was something in the middle.  Maybe a "Meh" option with a hand laid flat out like paper.  I'm sure with some time and updates and patches, this game will be phenomenal and I would expect I would give it a full "thumbs up."  As of right now, I can't really recommend this game since I feel I was lied to and a little bit cheated.

I understand the amazing undertaking Sean Murray and Hello Games got themselves into when developing No Man's Sky.  The idea of a procedurely generated universe is nothing short of total awesomeness.  I have been watching the development of the game since it was first announced in 2013.  The gameplay trailers showed graphics that were beautiful, the imagery was awe-inspiring and the compleyity of the life forms and ecosystems made me want this game more and more.  The space battles looked amazing and the option for multiplayer being dangled in front of me in this kind of setting was enough.  I had to have this game.

And now I have it.  Here's why I am disappointed:

The graphics are still pretty good.  The lighting on the planets is not the same as what I saw in the trailer, a little flat, but OK.  

The ecosystems on the procedurely generated planets all look the same to me.  I have been to a couple of dozen planets and all looked exactly the same.  The flora and fauna still looked exactly the same in different star systems and the terrain was pretty much identical exept for the atmosphere being hostile or not.  The fauna also looks pathetically hysterical.  I ran into a creature that had one foot of a slug, the body of a caterpillar, the frill of a flower around its neck and the face of a velociraptor.  It just hopped along in circles and was kind of discouraging.  I saw that thing on six of the planets I discovered.  

Where's the multiplayer?  

I understand this is an exploration and survival game, but there really isn't any reason for me to go into that cave over there because there is nothing inside there that I can't find outside the cave.  By the way, all caves look the same on all planets so far.  Also, for a survival game, there isn't much you can do at the beginning since you don't have many spots on your person or ship to save the things you need.  The resource management system definitely needs some tweaking.

Hello Games, please update and patch this game so it doesn't continue to feel like a $4.99 indie title.  I paid $60 for a AAA game.  Please deliver what you promised.

Reviews.203363:
I have never felt my time so wasted by a main quest in a game. The writing is poor, dialogue is vague and the game tells you that no matter what you do, your choice is pointless anyway. The biggest mystery in the game is not answered and your only choice is a massive disappointment. It takes a solid hour of warping towards the centre to complete the main quest, nothing more than open the map, jump to black hole, warp, repeat for a whole hour.

The game is in a decent playable state now (providing you completely ignore the main quest) but not without it's flaws. Progression both for quests and gear seems to make more sense now, systems work better together, there's lots of stuff to do and on the whole it's enjoyable to play. I tried a weekend community mission for the new cosmetic currency and it was absolute trash. 1.5 hours of trying to find scarce resources with other real players and bases everywhere breaking immersion and removing the terrain under mission objectives. However, base building is generally well done (several bugs still) and very similar to Subnautica's module method. You could visit dozens / hundreds of systems in a playthrough, but the teleporter system just lists them by name with absolutely NO way or sorting them, knowing what they contain or how close to galactic centre they are. Exploring is still wonderous, but seriously suffers by basically all trillions of planets being the same. Hopefully they learn their lessons from NMS and put it all together for a fantastic lie-free sequel.

Pros:
- The first time I found a completely wrecked ship and managed to repair all it's subsystems to get it flight-worthy again felt awesome
- Seamless transition between earth and sky
- Learning words so you can understand aliens is awesome
- Scanning and logging alien life is cool (but pointless)
- I really enjoy discovering new plants, but it feels really crap that once you've landed on a planet in one spot, you've seen the entire planet.
- Ocean planets and underwater exploration is now pretty great

Cons:
- View distance on planets is poor
- Textures sometimes stop loading
- Quests will not work unless you have one actively selected
- The main quest is split into two questlines at once, but you can only advance one of the two tasks at a time, and the game doesn't tell you which
- Constantly farming basic resources to charge life support, fuel & weapons is boring and grindy
- Every planet in the universe is the same, there's nothing uniquely interesting to explore. 
- Inventory management is constantly annoying. They've since added storage on your freighter, but accessing and organising it is clunky
- No manual takeoff/landing
- The language system is a repetetive grind (you learn one new word by repeating exactly the same 3 lines of dialogue with an NPC, 2000+ words)
- The UI and technology management is unintuitive
- Lots of the game's mechanics are never even mentioned inside the game and are left to the wiki or Reddit to explain
- Space combat is basic, starship controls are awful by default and only slightly better in alternate mode (which most people don't seem to know exists)
- Dialogue is generally so deliberately vague that you have no idea what's going on for most of the game
- The main quest line is ridiculous, suffers from the dialogue issue above and ends in a serious anti-climax

With a game like this, you have to make a decision at the start about how many planets you're going to have; a hand-crafted small number, or 'lots'. Although NMS boasts an enormous number of planets, it doesn't actually gain anything from it. Because there are 18 quintillion planets, none of them are special or interesting, and they simply become a resource to gather. I love exploring in games, but only when there's cool stuff to discover. The difference between NMS and Subnautica for example is that Subnautica's world is entirely hand-crafted, and literally everything you can find in it is cool and awe inspiring.

I will give credit to the developers, I have never seen so many free content updates after such a terrible launch and they deserve credit for that. They did, however, still lie through their teeth about the game before launch and I'd never pre-order anything from them. The result is a playable game that's still mostly devoid of anything uniquely interesting with various kinds of grinding mechanics that don't all work very well together and a massively disappointing ending.

What is there to say really...

This is the most I've been invested in a game in a while. I played during the launch week and put in a solid 50 hours, so I know how bad it was back then and I was annoyed despite getting my moneys worth in playtime at how much the game lacked. Sure there were fun moments but it got dried out when you realised what was missing and how aimless it was.

Now, with constant updates and further improvement from the Hello Games team I can safely say the game is not that anymore. It's a game I can really see myself hopping on for a few hours at a time here and there, completing more of the storyline which adds a whole new dynamic and seeing what each planet has to offer.

The game has always been beautiful even on launch (albeit buggy back then) but there is so much more to do now it's great. You can build on any planet anywhere you want, even underwater which is a nice new detail, there's now freighters which you can design to how you want while also managing that pesky storage, different guns wherever you go, a larger variety of ships and with every update something to always keep you on your toes - with constant updates and no looks to have it slowed down either I don't see why you wouldn't have got this game in it's current state.

The newest living ship update along with the ability to create pretty detailed music is just a number of the fun small things to do when you get bored of exploring or whatever mission you were on. 

The progression and pacing is perfect too, you don't get everything too quickly or from the start, you actually have to grind a bit and it can be sped up by focusing solely on that area, for instance you want to get a ship geared to more pirate runs and combat? You will want to focus on acquiring units and getting those blueprints and materials to install them. Want to make an awesome base with the 100's of options to craft? You will want to focus on digging up the buried technology so you can purchase as many of the building parts you need while focusing on the materials needed and your away.

Each thing you focus on to has endless hours or replayabilty, I don't see there being any real 'endgame' and with the multiplayer feature (something else that should have been there from the start), you can now hop on with your friends, build together, do missions and more!

Currently sitting at 57 hours invested in this game, however I can see that going up by a lot over the next year as there's just so much to do and I'm having a blast. I want to experience all of it. It's going to be hard catching up to date however with all these updates in place!

Reviews.210455:
Update, years later!

This game exceeds expectations even from my positive viewpoint from when it released, and my consensus now is that you need this game.

/////

It's finally here! And I wanted to give my review, even though I'm really only 16 hours in and there's lots more to discover and do, I also think this game deserves way more than a "mixed" reaction.

[h1]The good:[/h1]

[list]
    [*]The game runs pretty well, even though I'm on like a mid-range system with 8 gigs of ram, 2 gigs of gpu ram and a quadcore processor. I'd say I get anywhere from 30-50 FPS, which I don't think is terrible at all. I think that nowadays people are kind of spoiled when it comes to this aspect of gaming, considering 30 is absolutely fine and playable about 99.9% of the time.
    [*]The atmosphere beats other space themed games by far. The music is pretty awesome and the planets are really varied. There are some saying that all they've seen are the same iterations over and over, but remember, there are 18 quintillion planets and what you see is based on luck. You could start in a chain of systems with tons of dead planets, or a chain of system exploding with life. But here's a hint: If all you're getting is dead planets in your starter system, don't bother jumping to other systems, just start a new game and you'll end up somewhere new.
    [*]The survival aspects are at a perfect balance, in my opinion. I see some people saying it's really aggravating to have to manage all your systems but right from the get-go I never really had an issue with it? I just stay stocked on carbon, zinc,  plutonium and thamium9 and I never have any issues. What would be cool to see is possibly the need to eat and drink periodically.
    [*]While kind of difficult to get used to at first, the flight mechanics become nearly second nature and are more intuitive, easier to control than Elite: Dangerous.
    [*]Trading, while not extremely deep, is exactly what I would expect from a space sim survival game, and amassing a fortune is pretty dang fun, although I'm still waiting for someone to sell their ship to me at a reasonable price lol
    [*]Combat, while obviously not the main focus of the game, isn't too terrible and if you find yourself in a position where you need to defend yourself, it's pretty simple. This will happen a lot if you're like me and you're always hauling highly valuable goods.
    [*]Space! After watching a bunch of PS4 streams, I was afraid that space would be super condensed in color with no opportunity for star gazing, but in the very second or third system I entered, I found a system that was very traditionally space looking. See my screenshots for an example. Overall I think it's well-done.
[/list]

[h1]The bad:[/h1]

[list]
    [*]One of the only things I really have any issue with is the fact that the menus feel like they were copy/pasted directly from the console version. I don't mind having to hold down a button to toggle things but I think it needs some optimization before it feels right on the PC version.
    [*]There are NPCs to talk to through this neat text-adventure/Mass Effect-esque system in almost every system, but I feel like there could be more in certain places, like in the bars on space stations. It would only add to the atmosphere.
[/list]

Overall No Man's Sky is fudging great and, for me, exactly what I was waiting for.

No Man's Sky is terrific, maybe not a game for everyone, but I think after some tweaking this should definitely be game of the year. If you like space sims with survival aspects, you have no reason not to own this game.

[h1]A Masterclass in Both How and How Not to do PR[/h1]
I was one of the people who pre-ordered this game. I rode the hype train in the foremost cars, and when the game came out I was disappointed but still found things to enjoy. With Sony's help Sean Murray basically burned Hello Games' previously-flooded office to the ground with the release of this game, though unlike many people I doubt it was as intentional as it may or may not have seemed. Hello Games have worked tirelessly to repair the good will they shed with this game and they have seriously delivered everything they originally promised and more. You got your multiplayer, you got quests, you got base building ala something like Subnautica, you got space battles, trading, killing pirates, and perhaps most importantly, you got just exploring crazy worlds and creatures (both on foot and in vehicles now). Plus where else are you gonna find a game without DLC anymore?

Seriously. Seriously recommended.

- Discoveries sometimes don't register for other players. (ex. custom names)
- Quests sometimes don't sync with other players. Ex. you build a research station on a shared base and the other player still has to build one. On the flip side, sometimes it does sync.
- The most annoying glitch of all: sometimes when 2 players are landed near each other, it repeats the landing sound... forever... and loudly. Biggest literal headache.

Other than that, the updates they have made give you a massive sense of wonder and awe. I've also played this game in VR, which is an amazing experience. The only VR glitch I've seen is when looking at another VR players, their hands track very... weirdly. Waving your hands in the air is a good example of this, as the players arms appear to buckle in on themselves.

Don't let all the negative parts deter you, though. If you love space, you will love this game.
